rows.text: Schneider subdivides impulses (_Triebe_) into sensation-impulses, perception-impulses, and idea-impulses.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To crouch from cold is a sensation-impulse; to turn and follow, if we see people running one way, is a perception-impulse; to cast about for cover, if it begins to blow and rain, is an imagination-impulse.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: A single complex instinctive action may involve successively the awakening of impulses of all three classes.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Thus a hungry lion starts to _seek_ prey by the awakening in him of imagination coupled with desire; he begins to _stalk_ it when, on eye, ear, or nostril, he gets an impression of its presence at a certain distance; he _springs_ upon it, either when the booty takes alarm and flees, or when the distance is sufficiently reduced; he proceeds to _tear_ and _devour_ it the moment he gets a sensation of its contact with his claws and fangs.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Seeking, stalking, springing, and devouring are just so many different kinds of muscular contraction, and neither kind is called forth by the stimulus appropriate to the other.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Schneider says of the hamster, which stores corn in its hole:
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: "If we analyze the propensity of storing, we find that it consists of three impulses: First, an impulse to _pick up_ the nutritious object, due to perception; second, an impulse to _carry it off_ into the dwelling-place, due to the idea of this latter; and third, an impulse to _lay it down_ there, due to the sight of the place.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It lies in the nature of the hamster that it should never see a full ear of corn without feeling a desire to strip it; it lies in its nature to feel, as soon as its cheek-pouches are filled, an irresistible desire to hurry to its home; and finally, it lies in its nature that the sight of the storehouse should awaken the impulse to empty the cheeks" (p. 208).
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In certain animals of a low order the feeling of having executed one impulsive step is such an indispensable part of the stimulus of the next one, that the animal cannot make any variation in the order of its performance.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: _Now, why do the various animals do what seem to us such strange things,_ in the presence of such outlandish stimuli?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why does the hen, for example, submit herself to the tedium of incubating such a fearfully uninteresting set of objects as a nestful of eggs, unless she have some sort of a prophetic inkling of the result?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We can only interpret the instincts of brutes by what we know of instincts in ourselves.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why do men always lie down, when they can, on soft beds rather than on hard floors?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why, in a room, do they place themselves, ninety-nine times out of a hundred, with their faces towards its middle rather than to the wall?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why do they prefer saddle of mutton and champagne to hard-tack and ditch-water?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why does the maiden interest the youth so that everything about her seems more important and significant than anything else in the world?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Nothing more can be said than that these are human ways, and that every creature _likes_ its own ways, and takes to the following them as a matter of course.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Science may come and consider these ways, and find that most of them are useful.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But it is not for the sake of their utility that they are followed, but because at the moment of following them we feel that that is the only appropriate and natural thing to do.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Not one man in a billion, when taking his dinner, ever thinks of utility.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He eats because the food tastes good and makes him want more.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If you ask him _why_ he should want to eat more of what tastes like that, instead of revering you as a philosopher he will probably laugh at you for a fool.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The connection between the savory sensation and the act it awakens is for him absolute and _selbstverständlich_, an '_a priori_ synthesis' of the most perfect sort, needing no proof but its own evidence.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It takes, in short, what Berkeley calls a mind debauched by learning to carry the process of making the natural seem strange, so far as to ask for the _why_ of any instinctive human act.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To the metaphysician alone can such questions occur as: Why do we smile, when pleased, and not scowl?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Why are we unable to talk to a crowd as we talk to a single friend?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The common man can only say, "_Of course_ we smile, _of course_ our heart palpitates at the sight of the crowd, _of course_ we love the maiden, that beautiful soul clad in that perfect form, so palpably and flagrantly made from all eternity to be loved!"
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And so, probably, does each animal feel about the particular things it tends to do in presence of particular objects.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To the lion it is the lioness which is made to be loved; to the bear, the she-bear.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To the broody hen the notion would probably seem monstrous that there should be a creature in the world to whom a nestful of eggs was not the utterly fascinating and precious and never-to-be-too-much-sat-upon object which it is to her.[362]
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Thus we may be sure that, however mysterious some animals' instincts may appear to us, our instincts will appear no less mysterious to them.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And we may conclude that, to the animal which obeys it, every impulse and every step of every instinct shines with its own sufficient light, and seems at the moment the only eternally right and proper thing to do.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: What voluptuous thrill may not shake a fly, when she at last discovers the one particular leaf, or carrion, or bit of dung, that out of all the world can stimulate her ovipositor to its discharge?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Does not the discharge then seem to her the only fitting thing?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And need she care or know anything about the future maggot and its food?
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Since the _egg-laying instincts_ are simple examples to consider, a few quotations about them from Schneider may be serviceable:
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: "The phenomenon so often talked about, so variously interpreted, so surrounded with mystification, that an insect should always lay her eggs in a spot appropriate to the nourishment of her young, is no more marvellous than the phenomenon that every animal pairs with a mate capable of bearing posterity, or feeds on materials capable of affording him nourishment....
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Not only the choice of a place for laying the eggs, but all the various acts for depositing and protecting them, are occasioned by the perception of the proper object, and the relation of this perception to the various stages of maternal impulse.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When the burying beetle perceives a carrion, she is not only impelled to approach it and lodge her eggs in it, but also to go through the movements requisite for burying it; just us a bird who sees his hen-bird is impelled to caress her, to strut around her, dance before her, or in some other way to woo her; just as a tiger, when he sees an antelope, is impelled to stalk it, to pounce upon it, and to strangle it.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: "The perception of the empty nest, or of a single egg, seems in birds to stand in such a close relation to the physiological functions of oviparation, that it serves as a direct stimulus to these functions, while the perception of a sufficient number of eggs has just the opposite effect.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is well known that hens and ducks lay more eggs if we keep removing them than if we leave them in the nest.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The impulse to sit arises, as a rule, when a bird sees a certain number of eggs in her nest.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If this number is not yet to be seen there, the ducks continue to lay, although they perhaps have laid twice as many eggs as they are accustomed to sit upon....
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: That sitting, also, is independent of any idea of purpose and is a pure perception-impulse is evident, among other things, from the fact that many birds, e.g. wild ducks, steal eggs from each other....
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The bodily disposition to sit is, it is true, one condition [since broody hens will sit where there are no eggs], but the perception of the eggs is the other condition of the activity of the incubating impulse.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The propensity of the cuckoo and of the cow-bird to lay their eggs in the nests of other species must also be interpreted as a pure perception-impulse.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: These birds have no bodily disposition to become broody, and there is therefore in them no connection between the perception of an egg and the impulse to sit upon it.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Eggs ripen, however, in their oviducts, and the body tends to get rid of them.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And since the two birds just named do not drop their eggs anywhere on the ground, but in nests, which are the only places where they may preserve the species, it might easily appear that such preservation of the species was what they had in view, and that they acted with full consciousness of the purpose.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The cuckoo is simply excited by the perception of quite determinate sorts of nest, which already contain eggs, to drop her own into them, and throw the others out, because this perception is a direct stimulus to these acts.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is impossible that she should have any notion of the other bird coming and sitting on her egg."[363]
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Remember that nothing is said yet of the origin of instincts, but only of the constitution of those that exist fully formed.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Nothing is commoner than the remark that Man differs from lower creatures by the almost total absence of instincts, and the assumption of their work in him by 'reason.' A fruitless discussion might be waged on this point by two theorizers who were careful not to define their terms.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 'Reason' might be used, as it often has been, since Kant, not as the mere power of 'inferring,' but also as a name for the _tendency to obey impulses_ of a certain lofty sort, such as duty, or universal ends.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And 'instinct' might have its significance so broadened as to cover all impulses whatever, even the impulse to act from the idea of a distant fact, as well as the impulse to act from a present sensation.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Were the word instinct used in this broad way, it would of course be impossible to restrict it, as we began by doing, to actions done with no prevision of an end.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We must of course avoid a quarrel about words, and the facts of the case are really tolerably plain.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Man has a far greater variety of _impulses_ than any lower animal; and any one of these impulses, taken in itself, is as 'blind' as the lowest instinct can be; but, owing to man's memory, power of reflection, and power of inference, they come each one to be felt by him, after he has once yielded to them and experienced their results, in connection with a _foresight_ of those results.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In this condition an impulse acted out may be said to be acted out, in part at least, _for the sake_ of its results.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is obvious that _every instinctive act, in an animal with memory, must cease to be 'blind' after being once repeated,_ and must be accompanied with foresight of its 'end' just so far as that end may have fallen under the animal's cognizance.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: An insect that lays her eggs in a place where she never sees them hatched must always do so 'blindly;' but a hen who has already hatched a brood can hardly be assumed to sit with perfect 'blindness' on her second nest.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Some expectation of consequences must in every case like this be aroused; and this expectation, according as it is that of something desired or of something disliked, must necessarily either re-enforce or inhibit the mere impulse.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The hen's idea of the chickens would probably encourage her to sit; a rat's memory, on the other hand, of a former escape from a trap would neutralize his impulse to take bait from anything that reminded him of that trap.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If a boy sees a fat hopping-toad, he probably has incontinently an impulse (especially if with other boys) to smash the creature with a stone, which impulse we may suppose him blindly to obey.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But something in the expression of the dying toad's clasped hands suggests the meanness of the act, or reminds him of sayings he has heard about the sufferings of animals being like his own; so that, when next he is tempted by a toad, an idea arises which, far from spurring him again to the torment, prompts kindly actions, and may even make him the toad's champion against less reflecting boys.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is plain, then, that, _no matter how well endowed an animal may originally be in the way of instincts, his resultant actions will be much modified if the instincts combine with experience,_ if in addition to impulses he have memories, associations, inferences, and expectations, on any considerable scale.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: An object O, on which he has an instinctive impulse to react in the manner A, would _directly_ provoke him to that reaction.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But O has meantime become for him a _sign_ of the nearness of P, on which he has an equally strong impulse to react in the manner B, quite unlike A.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: So that when he meets O the immediate impulse A and the remote impulse B struggle in his breast for the mastery.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The fatality and uniformity said to be characteristic of instinctive actions will be so little manifest that one might be tempted to deny to him altogether the possession of any instinct about the object O.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The instinct about O is there; only by the complication of the associative machinery it has come into conflict with another instinct about P.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Here we immediately reap the good fruits of our simple physiological conception of what an instinct is.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If it be a mere excito-motor impulse, due to the pre-existence of a certain 'reflex arc' in the nerve-centres of the creature, of course it must follow the law of all such reflex arcs.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: One liability of such arcs is to have their activity 'inhibited,' by other processes going on at the same time.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It makes no difference whether the arc be organized at birth, or ripen spontaneously later, or be due to acquired habit, it must take its chances with all the other arcs, and sometimes succeed, and sometimes fail, in drafting off the currents through itself.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The physiological view would require it to show occasional irregularities in any animal in whom the number of separate instincts, and the possible entrance of the same stimulus into several of them, were great.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And such irregularities are what every superior animal's instincts do show in abundance.[364]
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Wherever the mind is elevated enough to discriminate; wherever several distinct sensory elements must combine to discharge the reflex-arc; wherever, instead of plumping into action instantly at the first rough intimation of what _sort_ of a thing is there, the agent waits to see which _one_ of its kind it is and what the _circumstances_ are of its appearance; wherever different individuals and different circumstances can impel him in different ways; wherever these are the conditions--we have a masking of the elementary constitution of the instinctive life.
rows.author: William James
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In presenting to the public these stories based on the folk-lore of the Gold Coast peoples, it seems necessary to say something in general terms of the economic and social development of the colony in so far as that development is affecting the ‘lore’ of the folk.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Not until the civilization and industrialism of Europe began to penetrate into the districts of the Guinea Coast was any great attempt made to study the folk-lore of these peoples.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is obvious, therefore, that the student must find considerable admixture from outside sources which the absence of a native system of writing and consequent literature makes exceedingly difficult to detect.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The difficulties increase with time, for we are getting farther and farther from the genuine folk-lore.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Each year, from towns like Accra, Seccondee, and Cape Coast the tentacles of European civilization are slowly extending in all directions.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Railways and roads are creeping out, old-fashioned crudity is giving way to simpler and more expeditious methods; new industries, as rubber and cocoa, are being established. [1] All this must be borne in mind in studying the folk-lore as told by the native to-day.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: What is happening is, unfortunately, not an awakening, but a transformation.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The negro is discarding his native cloth for a European suit of clothes.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: “On all sides it is reported that the demand for European provisions, luxuries, and apparel is large and greatly increasing.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The large imports of tinned provisions, flour, etc., is in part due to the scarcity of native food-stuffs in certain districts, but there is no doubt that the standard of living is changing and rising.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: “There is a general desire not only in the colony, but in Ashanti, for better roads, better houses, cleaner villages, and the desire has been prompted by the example of the great sanitary improvements in the larger towns....
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: “It can be observed that the people take a growing pride in the institutions and traditions of their country, that the chiefs are realizing the duties and influence of their position, and that public opinion, among the educated classes, at any rate, is beginning to recognize that some advance on the ideals and standards of the past must now be demanded.” [2]
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This, from the utilitarian and Imperial standpoints, is as it should be, but it tends to be fatal to the mythology, the customs, and the traditions of such peoples as the negroes of West Africa.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: For this change is not taking place only in the direction of mere materialism.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Christianity, entering the country through the ports, and Mohammedanism, being carried by Haussas along the trade routes from the interior, are playing their part in these psychological and sociological changes.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The negro of yesterday differs from the negro of to-day as he in turn will differ from the negro of to-morrow.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In view of all this metamorphosis it is much to be regretted that the geographical and linguistical difficulties have made the task of the folk-lorist not only difficult but wellnigh impossible.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Much, of course, might be done if those whose duties carry them into the various districts would take in hand the task.
rows.author: Collected by W. H. Barker; illustrated by Cecilia Sinclair

rows.text: The collation of their results might enable one to eradicate outside and recent influences and in a measure get at “the back of the black man’s mind.”

rows.text: The Cherokee were the mountaineers of the South, holding the entire Allegheny region from the interlocking head-streams of the Kanawha and the Tennessee southward almost to the site of Atlanta, and from the Blue ridge on the east to the Cumberland range on the west, a territory comprising an area of about 40,000 square miles, now included in the states of Virginia, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama.

rows.text: Their principal towns were upon the headwaters of the Savannah, Hiwassee, and Tuckasegee, and along the whole length of the Little Tennessee to its junction with the main stream.

rows.text: Itsâti, or Echota, on the south bank of the Little Tennessee, a few miles above the mouth of Tellico river, in Tennessee, was commonly considered the capital of the Nation.

rows.text: As the advancing whites pressed upon them from the east and northeast the more exposed towns were destroyed or abandoned and new settlements were formed lower down the Tennessee and on the upper branches of the Chattahoochee and the Coosa.

rows.text: As is always the case with tribal geography, there were no fixed boundaries, and on every side the Cherokee frontiers were contested by rival claimants.

rows.text: In Virginia, there is reason to believe, the tribe was held in check in early days by the Powhatan and the Monacan.

rows.text: On the east and southeast the Tuscarora and Catawba were their inveterate enemies, with hardly even a momentary truce within the historic period; and evidence goes to show that the Sara or Cheraw were fully as hostile.

rows.text: On the south there was hereditary war with the Creeks, who claimed nearly the whole of upper Georgia as theirs by original possession, but who were being gradually pressed down toward the Gulf until, through the mediation of the United States, a treaty was finally made fixing the boundary between the two tribes along a line running about due west from the mouth of Broad river on the Savannah.

rows.text: Toward the west, the Chickasaw on the lower Tennessee and the Shawano on the Cumberland repeatedly turned back the tide of Cherokee invasion from the rich central valleys, while the powerful Iroquois in the far north set up an almost unchallenged claim of paramount lordship from the Ottawa river of Canada southward at least to the Kentucky river.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: On the other hand, by their defeat of the Creeks and expulsion of the Shawano, the Cherokee made good the claim which they asserted to all the lands from upper Georgia to the Ohio river, including the rich hunting grounds of Kentucky.

rows.text: Holding as they did the great mountain barrier between the English settlements on the coast and the French or Spanish garrisons along the Mississippi and the Ohio, their geographic position, no less than their superior number, would have given them the balance of power in the South but for a looseness of tribal organization in striking contrast to the compactness of the Iroquois league, by which for more than a century the French power was held in check in the north.

rows.text: The English, indeed, found it convenient to recognize certain chiefs as supreme in the tribe, but the only real attempt to weld the whole Cherokee Nation into a political unit was that made by the French agent, Priber, about 1736, which failed from its premature discovery by the English.

rows.text: The proper name by which the Cherokee call themselves (1) [1] is Yûñ'wiya', or Ani'-Yûñ'wiya' in the third person, signifying "real people," or "principal people," a word closely related to Oñwe-hoñwe, the name by which the cognate Iroquois know themselves.

rows.text: The most ancient tradition concerning the Cherokee appears to be the Delaware tradition of the expulsion of the Talligewi from the north, as first noted by the missionary Heckewelder in 1819, and published more fully by Brinton in the Walam Olum in 1885.

rows.text: According to the first account, the Delawares, advancing from the west, found their further progress opposed by a powerful people called Alligewi or Talligewi, occupying the country upon a river which Heckewelder thinks identical with the Mississippi, but which the sequel shows was more probably the upper Ohio.

rows.text: The Delawares decide upon war and call in the help of their northern friends, the "Talamatan," i. e., the Wyandot and other allied Iroquoian tribes.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: A war ensues which continues through the terms of four successive chiefs, when victory declares for the invaders, and "all the Talega go south." The country is then divided, the Talamatan taking the northern portion, while the Delawares "stay south of the lakes." The chronicle proceeds to tell how, after eleven more chiefs have ruled, the Nanticoke and Shawano separate from the parent tribe and remove to the south.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Six other chiefs follow in succession until we come to the seventh, who "went to the Talega mountains." By this time the Delawares have reached the ocean.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Other chiefs succeed, after whom "the Easterners and the Wolves"--probably the Mahican or Wappinger and the Munsee--move off to the northeast.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: At last, after six more chiefs, "the whites came on the eastern sea," by which is probably meant the landing of the Dutch on Manhattan in 1609 (7).
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We may consider this a tally date, approximating the beginning of the seventeenth century.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Two more chiefs rule, and of the second we are told that "He fought at the south; he fought in the land of the Talega and Koweta," and again the fourth chief after the coming of the whites "went to the Talega." We have thus a traditional record of a war of conquest carried on against the Talligewi by four successive chiefs, and a succession of about twenty-five chiefs between the final expulsion of that tribe and the appearance of the whites, in which interval the Nanticoke, Shawano, Mahican, and Munsee branched off from the parent tribe of the Delawares.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Without venturing to entangle ourselves in the devious maze of Indian chronology, it is sufficient to note that all this implies a very long period of time--so long, in fact, that during it several new tribes, each of which in time developed a distinct dialect, branch off from the main Lenape' stem.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is distinctly stated that all the Talega went south after their final defeat; and from later references we find that they took refuge in the mountain country in the neighborhood of the Koweta (the Creeks), and that Delaware war parties were still making raids upon both these tribes long after the first appearance of the whites.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Although at first glance it might be thought that the name Tallige-wi is but a corruption of Tsalagi, a closer study leads to the opinion that it is a true Delaware word, in all probability connected with waloh or walok, signifying a cave or hole (Zeisberger), whence we find in the Walam Olum the word oligonunk rendered as "at the place of caves." It would thus be an exact Delaware rendering of the same name, "people of the cave country," by which, as we have seen, the Cherokee were commonly known among the tribes.
rows.author: Collected by James Mooney from named Cherokee sources and communities
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 2. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Always without desire we must be found, If its deep mystery we would sound; But if desire always within us be, Its outer fringe is all that we shall see.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different names.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what the want of skill is.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: So it is that existence and non-existence give birth the one to (the idea of) the other; that difficulty and ease produce the one (the idea of) the other; that length and shortness fashion out the one the figure of the other; that (the ideas of) height and lowness arise from the contrast of the one with the other; that the musical notes and tones become harmonious through the relation of one with another; and that being before and behind give the idea of one following another.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the sage manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All things spring up, and there is not one which declines to show itself; they grow, and there is no claim made for their ownership; they go through their processes, and there is no expectation (of a reward for the results).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The work is accomplished, and there is no resting in it (as an achievement).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
theme_evidence: Đã đọc toàn văn dòng; chủ đề xét theo ý chính, chưa xác minh nguồn/quyền để Release.
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The work is done, but how no one can see; 'Tis this that makes the power not cease to be.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to keep the people from rivalry among themselves; not to prize articles which are difficult to procure is the way to keep them from becoming thieves; not to show them what is likely to excite their desires is the way to keep their minds from disorder.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the sage, in the exercise of his government, empties their minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He constantly (tries to) keep them without knowledge and without desire, and where there are those who have knowledge, to keep them from presuming to act (on it).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When there is this abstinence from action, good order is universal.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: How deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: How pure and still the Tao is, as if it would ever so continue!
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The sages do not act from (any wish to be) benevolent; they deal with the people as the dogs of grass are dealt with.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'Tis moved again, and sends forth air the more.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Much speech to swift exhaustion lead we see; Your inner being guard, and keep it free.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; The female mystery thus do we name.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, Is called the root from which grew heaven and earth.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Long and unbroken does its power remain, Used gently, and without the touch of pain.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The reason why heaven and earth are able to endure and continue thus long is because they do not live of, or for, themselves.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; he treats his person as if it were foreign to him, and yet that person is preserved.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Is it not because he has no personal and private ends, that therefore such ends are realised?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The excellence of a residence is in (the suitability of) the place; that of the mind is in abysmal stillness; that of associations is in their being with the virtuous; that of government is in its securing good order; that of (the conduct of) affairs is in its ability; and that of (the initiation of) any movement is in its timeliness.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And when (one with the highest excellence) does not wrangle (about his low position), no one finds fault with him.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When the intelligent and animal souls are held together in one embrace, they can be kept from separating.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When one gives undivided attention to the (vital) breath, and brings it to the utmost degree of pliancy, he can become as a (tender) babe.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When he has cleansed away the most mysterious sights (of his imagination), he can become without a flaw.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In loving the people and ruling the state, cannot he proceed without any (purpose of) action?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the opening and shutting of his gates of heaven, cannot he do so as a female bird?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: While his intelligence reaches in every direction, cannot he (appear to) be without knowledge?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 3. (The Tao) produces (all things) and nourishes them; it produces them and does not claim them as its own; it does all, and yet does not boast of it; it presides over all, and yet does not control them.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This is what is called 'The mysterious Quality' (of the Tao).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Colour's five hues from th' eyes their sight will take; Music's five notes the ears as deaf can make; The flavours five deprive the mouth of taste; The chariot course, and the wild hunting waste Make mad the mind; and objects rare and strange, Sought for, men's conduct will to evil change.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the sage seeks to satisfy (the craving of) the belly, and not the (insatiable longing of the) eyes.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He puts from him the latter, and prefers to seek the former.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and great calamity, to be regarded as personal conditions (of the same kind).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Disgrace is being in a low position (after the enjoyment of favour).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The getting that (favour) leads to the apprehension (of losing it), and the losing it leads to the fear of (still greater calamity):--this is what is meant by saying that favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And what is meant by saying that honour and great calamity are to be (similarly) regarded as personal conditions?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: What makes me liable to great calamity is my having the body (which I call myself); if I had not the body, what great calamity could come to me?
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore he who would administer the kingdom, honouring it as he honours his own person, may be employed to govern it, and he who would administer it with the love which he bears to his own person may be entrusted with it.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the Equable.' We listen to it, and we do not hear it, and we name it 'the Inaudible.' We try to grasp it, and do not get hold of it, and we name it 'the Subtle.' With these three qualities, it cannot be made the subject of description; and hence we blend them together and obtain The One.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Its upper part is not bright, and its lower part is not obscure.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Ceaseless in its action, it yet cannot be named, and then it again returns and becomes nothing.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This is called the Form of the Formless, and the Semblance of the Invisible; this is called the Fleeting and Indeterminable.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it, and do not see its Back.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle and exquisite penetration, comprehended its mysteries, and were deep (also) so as to elude men's knowledge.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As they were thus beyond men's knowledge, I will make an effort to describe of what sort they appeared to be.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Shrinking looked they like those who wade through a stream in winter; irresolute like those who are afraid of all around them; grave like a guest (in awe of his host); evanescent like ice that is melting away; unpretentious like wood that has not been fashioned into anything; vacant like a valley, and dull like muddy water.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They who preserve this method of the Tao do not wish to be full (of themselves).
rows.author: Laozi; translated by James Legge
rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is through their not being full of themselves that they can afford to seem worn and not appear new and complete.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To know that unchanging rule is to be intelligent; not to know it leads to wild movements and evil issues.

rows.text: The knowledge of that unchanging rule produces a (grand) capacity and forbearance, and that capacity and forbearance lead to a community (of feeling with all things).

rows.text: From this community of feeling comes a kingliness of character; and he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Possessed of the Tao, he endures long; and to the end of his bodily life, is exempt from all danger of decay.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'

rows.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it would be better for the people a hundredfold.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But mark their issues, good and ill;-- What space the gulf between shall fill?

rows.text: 'Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?'

rows.text: There have been none, who, not liking to offend against their superiors, have been fond of stirring up confusion. 2.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: That being established, all practical courses naturally grow up.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Filial piety and fraternal submission!-- are they not the root of all benevolent actions?' CHAP.

rows.text: The Master said, 'Fine words and an insinuating appearance are seldom associated with true virtue.' CHAP.

rows.text: The philosopher Tsang said, 'I daily examine myself on three points:-- whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful;-- whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere;-- whether I may have not mastered and practised the instructions of my teacher.'
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'A youth, when at home, should be filial, and, abroad, respectful to his elders.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When he has time and opportunity, after the performance of these things, he should employ them in polite studies.' CHAP.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Tsze-hsia said, 'If a man withdraws his mind from the love of beauty, and applies it as sincerely to the love of the virtuous; if, in serving his parents, he can exert his utmost strength;

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: if, in serving his prince, he can devote his life; if, in his intercourse with his friends, his words are sincere:-- although men say that he has not learned, I will certainly say that he has.' CHAP.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'If the scholar be not grave, he will not call forth any veneration, and his learning will not be solid. 2.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The philosopher Tsang said, 'Let there be a careful attention to perform the funeral rites to parents, and let them be followed when long gone with the ceremonies of sacrifice;-- then the virtue of the people will resume its proper excellence.'

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Tsze-ch'in asked Tsze-kung, saying, 'When our master comes to any country, he does not fail to learn all about its government.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Tsze-kung said, 'Our master is benign, upright, courteous, temperate, and complaisant, and thus he gets his information.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The master's mode of asking information!-- is it not different from that of other men?' CHAP.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'While a man's father is alive, look at the bent of his will; when his father is dead, look at his conduct.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If for three years he does not alter from the way of his father, he may be called filial.'
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The philosopher Yu said, 'In practising the rules of propriety, a natural ease is to be prized.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the ways prescribed by the ancient kings, this is the excellent quality, and in things small and great we follow them. 2.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If one, knowing how such ease should be prized, manifests it, without regulating it by the rules of propriety, this likewise is not to be done.' CHAP.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The philosopher Yu said, 'When agreements are made according to what is right, what is spoken can be made good.
