rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When respect is shown according to what is proper, one keeps far from shame and disgrace.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When the parties upon whom a man leans are proper persons to be intimate with, he can make them his guides and masters.' CHAP.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: in his dwelling place does he seek the appliances of ease; he is earnest in what he is doing, and careful in his speech; he frequents the company of men of principle that he may be rectified:-- such a person may be said indeed to love to learn.' CHAP.

rows.text: Tsze-kung said, 'What do you pronounce concerning the poor man who yet does not flatter, and the rich man who is not proud?' The Master replied, 'They will do; but they are not equal to him, who, though poor, is yet cheerful, and to him, who, though rich, loves the rules of propriety.' 2.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. 2.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 'If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.' CHAP.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. 2.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 'At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. 6.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: 'At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.' CHAP.

rows.text: Soon after, as Fan Ch'ih was driving him, the Master told him, saying, 'Mang-sun asked me what filial piety was, and I answered him,-- "not being disobedient."' 3.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If, when their elders have any troublesome affairs, the young take the toil of them, and if, when the young have wine and food, they set them before their elders, is THIS to be considered filial piety?'

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'The accomplished scholar is not a utensil.' CHAP.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.' CHAP.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'The superior man is catholic and no partisan.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Master said, 'Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.' CHAP.
rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.author: Confucius; translated by James Legge
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When one gives few occasions for blame in his words, and few occasions for repentance in his conduct, he is in the way to get emolument.'

rows.text: The Duke Ai asked, saying, 'What should be done in order to secure the submission of the people?' Confucius replied, 'Advance the upright and set aside the crooked, then the people will submit.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Let him advance the good and teach the incompetent;-- then they will eagerly seek to be virtuous.' CHAP.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Emil Schlagintweit has given “An alphabetical list of the books and memoirs connected with Buddhism.” Although not completely exhaustive, it occupies thirty-five pages, and contains references to more than a hundred separate works, and a much larger number of essays and other literary articles.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Of those books and articles, the titles of about sixty allude to Tibet.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To them may be referred readers who wish for detailed information about that country, its literature, and its religion.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All that it is proposed to do here is to say a few words about the Tibetan work from which have been extracted the tales contained in the present volume; to give a short account of the enthusiastic Hungarian scholar, Csoma Körösi, who had so much to do with making that work known to Europe; and to call attention to any features which the stories now before us may have in common with European folk-tales.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To do more, without merely repeating what has been already said, would require a rare amount of special knowledge; and it may safely be asserted that remarks about Buddhism, made by writers who do not possess such knowledge, are seldom of signal value.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The tales contained in the sacred books of Tibet, it may be as well to remark at the outset, appear to have little that is specially Tibetan about them except their language.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Stories possessing characteristic features and suffused with local colour may possibly live in the memories of the natives of that region of lofty and bleak table-lands, with which so few Europeans have had an opportunity of becoming familiar.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But the legends and fables which the late Professor Schiefner has translated from the Kah-gyur are merely Tibetan versions of Sanskrit writings.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: No mention is made in them of those peculiarities of Tibetan Buddhism which have most struck the fancy of foreign observers.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Rhys Davids, “the Buddhism of Nepāl and Tibet differs from the Buddhism of Ceylon as much as the Christianity of Rome or of Moscow differs from that of Scotland or Wales.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But,” he proceeds to say, “the history of Buddhism from its commencement to its close is an epitome of the religious history of mankind.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And we have not solved the problem of Buddhism when we have understood the faith of the early Buddhists.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is in this respect that the study of later Buddhism in Ceylon, Burma, and Siam, in Nepāl and in Tibet, in China, Mongolia, and Japan, is only second in importance to the study of early Buddhism.”
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If children were born, they came into the world blind; fruits and grain came to nothing; cattle plague, famine, and pestilence prevailed; and of unavoidable misery was there much.” But after forty years had passed, there came five strangers to the king and said, “Great king, how couldst thou let these objects, so mystic and powerful, be cast into the treasury?” Having thus spoken, they suddenly disappeared.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the king ordered the holy objects to be brought forth from the treasury, and to be attached to the points of standards, and treated with the utmost respect and reverence.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: After that all went well: the king became prosperous and long-lived, children were born beautiful, famine and pestilence came to an end, and in their place appeared happiness and welfare.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: With the date of this event Sanang Setsen connects the introduction of Buddhism into Tibet; but according to Tibetan historians, says Schlagintweit, “the earliest period of the propagation of Buddhism, which reached down till the end of the tenth century A.D., begins with King Srongtsan Gampo, who was born in the year 617 A.D., and died 698.” This king is said to have sent a mission to India in the year 632 A.D., the result of which was the invention of a Tibetan alphabet, based upon Devanāgari characters, and the translation into Tibetan of Indian sacred books.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In his introduction of Buddhism into his kingdom he is said to have been “most energetically supported by his two wives, one of whom was a Nepalese, the other a Chinese princess.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Both of them, who throughout their lifetime proved most faithful votaries to the faith of Buddha, are worshipped either under the general name of Dolma (in Sanskrit Tārā), or under the respective names of Dolkar and Doljang.” After making considerable progress during the reign of this monarch, the new religion lost ground under his immediate successors.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Buddhism began to revive, owing to the useful regulations proclaimed by this king.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He it was who successfully crushed an attempt made by the chiefs during his minority to suppress the new creed, and it is principally due to him that the Buddhist faith became henceforth permanently established.”
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Towards the end of the ninth century, continues Schlagintweit, Buddhism was strongly opposed by a ruler who “commanded all temples and monasteries to be demolished, the images to be destroyed, and the sacred books to be burnt;” and his son and successor is also said to have died “without religion;” but his grandson was favourably inclined towards Buddhism, and rebuilt eight temples.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: “With this period we have to connect ‘the second propagation of Buddhism;’ it received, especially from the year 971 A.D., a powerful impetus from the joint endeavours of the returned Tibetan priests (who had fled the country under the preceding kings), and of the learned Indian priest Pandita Atisha and his pupil Brom-ston.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Shortly before Atisha came to Tibet, 1041 A.D., the Kāla Chakra doctrine, or Tantrika mysticism, was introduced into Tibet, and in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries many Indian refugees settled in the country, who greatly assisted the Tibetans in the translation of Sanskrit books.” It is probably from this period that the Kah-gyur dates.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the fourteenth century arose the reformer Tsonkhapa, who “imposed upon himself the difficult task of uniting and reconciling the dialectical and mystical schools which Tibetan Buddhism had brought forth, and also of eradicating the abuses gradually introduced by the priests.” Tradition asserts that he “had some intercourse with a stranger from the West, who was remarkable for a long nose.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Huc believes this stranger to have been a European missionary, and connects the resemblance of the religious service in Tibet to the Roman Catholic ritual with the information which Tsonkhapa might have received from this Roman Catholic priest.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We are not yet able to decide the question as to how far Buddhism may have borrowed from Christianity; but the rites of the Buddhists enumerated by the French missionary can for the most part either be traced back to institutions peculiar to Buddhism, or they have sprung up in periods posterior to Tsonkhapa.” [6]
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Rhys Davids has remarked that, “As in India, after the expulsion of Buddhism, the degrading worship of Śiva and his dusky bride had been incorporated into Brahmanism from the wild and savage devil-worship of the dark non-Aryan tribes, so as pure Buddhism died away in the North, the Tantra system, a mixture of magic and witchcraft and Śiva-worship, was incorporated into the corrupted Buddhism.” [7] Of this change for the worse, evidence about which there can be no mistake is supplied by the Tibetan sacred books.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Malan, who has made himself acquainted with the contents of some of their volumes in the original, says, [8] “There are passages of great beauty and great good sense, the most abstruse metaphysics, and the most absurd and incredible stories; yet not worse than those told in the Talmud, which equal or even surpass them in absurdity.”
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: On New Year’s day 1820, a traveller started from Bucharest on an adventurous journey towards the East.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: His name was Alexander Csoma Körösi (or de Körös), [9] and he was one of the sons of a Szekler military family of Eger-patak, in the Transylvanian circle of Hungary.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In 1799, when he seems to have been about nine years old, [10] he was sent to the Protestant College at Nagy-Enyed, where he studied for many years with the idea of taking orders.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In 1815 he was sent to Germany, and there he studied for three years, chiefly at the University of Göttingen, where he attended the lectures of the celebrated Orientalist Johann Gottfried Eichhorn.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: After his return from Germany, he spent the greater part of the year 1819 in studying various Slavonic dialects, first at Temesvar in Lower Hungary, then at Agram in Croatia.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But he soon resolved to apply himself to less-known tongues.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: “Among other liberal pursuits,” he wrote in 1825, [11] “my favourite studies were philology, geography, and history.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Although my ecclesiastical studies had prepared me for an honourable employment in my native country, yet my inclination for the studies above-mentioned induced me to seek a wider field for their future cultivation.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As my parents were dead, and my only brother did not want my assistance, I resolved to leave my native country and to come towards the East, and, by some means or other procuring subsistence, to devote my whole life to researches which may be afterwards useful in general to the learned world of Europe, and in particular may illustrate some obscure facts in ancient history.” Having no hope, he says, of obtaining “an imperial passport” for his journey, he procured “a printed Hungarian passport at Nagy-Enyed, to come on some pretended business to Bucharest,” intending to study Turkish there and then to go on to Constantinople.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But he could obtain neither instruction in Turkish nor the means of going direct to Constantinople.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: So he set forth from Bucharest on the 1st of January 1820, and travelled with some Bulgarian companions to Philippopolis.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Tidings of plague forced him to turn aside to the coast of the Archipelago, whence he sailed in a Greek ship to Alexandria.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Driven from that city by the plague, he made his way by sea to the coast of Syria, and thence on foot to Aleppo.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: From that city he proceeded to Bagdad, which he reached in July, travelling part of the way on foot, “with different caravans from various places, in an Asiatic dress,” and the rest “by water on a raft.” In September he left Bagdad, travelling in European costume on horseback with a caravan, and in the middle of next month he arrived at Teheran.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In March 1821 he again started with a caravan, travelling as an Armenian, and, after a stay of six months in Khorasán, arrived in the middle of November at Bokhara.
rows.author: Translated from Tibetan by F. Anton von Schiefner; English by W. R. S. Ralston
rows.work: Tibetan Tales, Derived from Indian Sources
