rows.text: While some of the provincial capitals are said to contain more people and to be more celebrated for certain reasons, Seoul is the home of the King and the Mecca of his faithful subjects.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The capital is a city of some 300,000 inhabitants, half of whom, perhaps, live in the extensive suburbs without the walls.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It lies in a basin of granite sand, surrounded by high mountains and their projecting ridges, over which climbs the high, thick, encircling wall of masonry; pierced at convenient points by massive, pagoda-roofed gates, amply strong enough for defense against the weapons of war in use at the time of building this great relic of seclusion.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The city is traversed by broad avenues from which runs a perfect labyrinth of narrow streets.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Originally none of these streets were less than twenty feet wide, and some of the avenues leading up to the imposing gates of the palaces are even now a good two hundred feet in width.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But the streets have all been encroached upon by the little temporary thatched booths of the petty retail dealers, so that, with the exception of the approaches to the palaces, the line is broken, the streets made tortuous, and only here and there a broad open spot indicates the original width of the thoroughfare.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Originally every street was furnished with its sewer--open in the smaller streets, while the avenues were drained by great covered sewers of stonework.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Occasionally the proprietor of one of the little temporary booths would put a foundation under his structure, bridging over the sewer, until now the streets have in many cases become mere crooked alleys, and but for the bountiful rains, the excellent natural drainage, and the character of the soil, the mortality would be very great instead of being less than in ordinary American cities.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: No attempt is made towards street decoration, as that would attract the attention of thieves.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The magnificent grounds of a nobleman, with their artificial lakes, flower gardens, water-worn pillars of ancient rock and quaintly twisted trees, may be enclosed by a row of tumble-down, smoke-begrimed servant-quarters that would never indicate the beauty to be found hidden within its forbidding exterior.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Travellers never seem to realize that a street in the East is apt to be but a "way" between two points, and as the usual Oriental odors greet their nostrils and their eyes rest on the dirty servants and their dirtier hovels, they at once denounce the whole town.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: There is attraction enough, however, in a Korean street for any one who is in search of strange sights.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Looking down one of the broad thoroughfares of Seoul from a point on the city wall, the sun's rays, falling on the light-colored gowns of the pedestrians as they saunter along amid the bulls and ponies, produce a kaleidoscopic effect that is certainly charming.
rows.author: Translated from Korean folklore by Horace Newton Allen
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: From time to time since the American occupation of the Islands, Philippine folk-tales have appeared in scientific publications, but never, so far as the writer is aware, has there been an attempt to offer to the general public a comprehensive popular collection of this material.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is my earnest hope that this collection of tales will give those who are interested opportunity to learn something of the magic, superstitions, and weird customs of the Filipinos, and to feel the charm of their wonder-world as it is pictured by these dark-skinned inhabitants of our Island possessions.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In company with my husband, who was engaged in ethnological work for the Field Museum of Natural History, it was my good fortune to spend four years among the wild tribes of the Philippines, During this time we frequently heard these stories, either related by the people in their homes and around the camp fires or chanted by the pagan priests in communion with the spirits.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The tales are now published in this little volume, with the addition of a few folk-legends that have appeared in the _Journal of American Folk-Lore_ and in scientific publications, here retold with some additions made by native story-tellers.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: I have endeavored to select typical tales from tribes widely separated and varying in culture from savagery to a rather high degree of development.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The stories are therefore divided into five groups, as follows: Tinguian, Igorot, the Wild Tribes of Mindanao, Moro, and Christian,
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The first two groups, Tinguian and Igorot, are from natives who inhabit the rugged mountain region of northwestern Luzon.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: From time immemorial they have been zealous head-hunters, and the stories teem with references to customs and superstitions connected with their savage practices.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In order to appreciate these tales to the fullest extent, we must understand the point of view of the Tinguian.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To him they embody all the known traditions of "the first times"--of the people who inhabited the earth before the present race appeared, of the ancient heroes and their powers and achievements.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In them he finds an explanation of and reason for many of his present laws and customs.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: A careful study of the whole body of Tinguian mythology points to the conclusion that the chief characters of these tales are not celestial beings but typical, generalized heroes of former ages, whose deeds have been magnified in the telling by many generations of their descendants.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They talked with jars, created human beings out of betel-nuts, raised the dead, and had the power of changing themselves into other forms.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This, however, does not seem strange or impossible to the Tinguian of today, for even now they talk with jars, perform certain rites to bring sickness and death to their foes, and are warned by omens received through the medium of birds, thunder and lightning, or the condition of the liver of a slaughtered animal.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They still converse freely with certain spirits who during religious ceremonies are believed to use the bodies of men or women as mediums for the purpose of advising and instructing the people.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Sometimes they go under different names, but in the minds of the story-tellers their personality and relationships are definitely established.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Thus Ini-init of the first tale becomes Kadayadawan in the second, Aponitolau in the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth, and Ligi in the seventh.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Kanag, the son of Aponitolau and Aponibolinayen, in the fifth tale is called Dumalawi.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: These heroes had most unusual relations with the heavenly bodies, all of which seem to have been regarded as animate beings.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the fourth tale Aponitolau marries Gaygayoma, the star maiden who is the daughter of the big star and the moon.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the first story the same character under the name of Ini-init seems to be a sun-god: we are told that he is "the sun," and again "a round stone which rolls." Thereupon we might conclude that he is a true solar being; yet in the other tales of this collection and in many more known to the Tinguian he reveals no celestial qualities.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Even in the first story he abandons his place in the sky and goes to live on earth.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the first eight stories we read of many customs of "the first times" which differ radically from those of the present.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But a careful analysis of all the known lore of this people points to the belief that many of these accounts depict a period when similar customs did exist among the people, or else were practiced by emigrants who generations ago became amalgamated with the Tinguian and whose strange customs finally became attributed to the people of the tales.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The stories numbered nine to sixteen are of a somewhat different type, and in them the Tinguian finds an explanation of many things, such as, how the people learned to plant, and to cure diseases, where they secured the valuable jars and beads, and why the moon has spots on its face.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All these stories are fully believed, the beads and jars are considered precious, and the places mentioned are definitely known.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: While the accounts seem to be of fairly recent origin they conflict neither with the fundamental ideas and traditions of "the first times" nor with the beliefs of today.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Stories seventeen to twenty-three are regarded as fables and are told to amuse the children or to while away the midday hours when the people seek shaded spots to lounge or stop on the trail to rest.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Most of them are known to the Christianized tribes throughout the Islands and show great similarity to the tales found in the islands to the south and, in some cases, in Europe.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In many of them the chief incidents are identical with those found elsewhere, but the story-tellers, by introducing old customs and beliefs, have moulded and colored them until they reflect the common ideas of the Tinguian.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The third group includes stories from several wild tribes who dwell in the large island of Mindanao.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Here are people who work in brass and steel, build good dwellings, and wear hemp clothing elaborately decorated with beads, shell disks, and embroidery, but who still practice many savage customs, including slavery and human sacrifice.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The fourth division gives two tales from the Moro (hardy Malayan warriors whose ancestors early became converts to the faith of Mohammed).
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Their teachers were the Arabian traders who, about 1400, succeeded in converting many of the Malay Islanders to the faith of the prophet.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The last group contains the stories of the Christianized natives--those who accepted the rule of Spain and with it the Catholic religion.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Their tales, while full of local color, nevertheless show the influence of the European tutors.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They furnish an excellent opportunity to contrast the literature of the savage head-hunters with that of the Moro and Christian tribes and to observe how various recent influences have modified the beliefs of people who not many centuries ago were doubtless of a uniform grade of culture.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is interesting, too, to note that European tales brought into the Islands by Mohammedan and Christian rulers and traders have been worked over until, at first glance, they now appear indigenous.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Still we find many incidents which are held in common by all the tribes of the Archipelago and even by the people of Borneo, Java, Sumatra, and India.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Some of these similarities and parallelisms are indicated in the foot-notes throughout the book.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The dim light of stars filtered through the leafy canopy above us, and the shadowy form of our guide once more appeared at my horse's head.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It was only for an instant, however, and then we were plunged again into the inky darkness of a tropical jungle.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We had planned to reach the distant Tinguian village in the late afternoon, but had failed to reckon with the deliberateness of native carriers.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It was only by urging our horses that we were able to ford the broad Abra ere the last rays of the sun dropped behind the mountains.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And then, in this land of no twilights, night had settled quickly over us.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We had made our way up the mountain-side, through the thick jungle, only to find that the trail, long imperceptible to us, had escaped even the keen eyes of our guide.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: On and on we went, through narrow paths, steep in places, and made rough and dangerous by sharp rocks as well as by those long creepers of the jungle whose thorny fingers are ever ready to seize horse or rider.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Occasionally we came out of the forest, only to cross rocky mountain streams; or perhaps it was the same stream that we crossed many times.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Our horses, becoming weary and uncertain of foot, grew more and more reluctant to plunge into the dark, swiftly flowing water.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: And our patience was nearly exhausted when we at last caught sight of dim lights in the valley below.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Coming out of the darkness, we were almost convinced that we had entered a new world.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Against the blackness of the night, grass-roofed houses stood outlined in the dim light of a bonfire; and squatting around that fire, unclad save for gay blankets wrapped about their shoulders, were brown-skinned men smoking long pipes, while women bedecked with bright beads were spinning cotton.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As they worked in the flickering light, they stretched their distaffs at arm's length into the air like witches waving their wands; and with that the elfland picture was complete.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the stillness of the night a single voice could be heard reciting some tale in a singsong tone, which was interrupted only when peals of laughter burst forth from the listeners, or when a scrawny dog rose to bark at an imaginary noise until the shouts of the men quieted him and he returned to his bed in the warm ashes.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Later we learned that these were the regular social gatherings of the Tinguian, and every night during the dry season one or more of these bonfires were to be seen in the village.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: After we had attained to the footing of welcome guests in these circles, we found that a good story-teller was always present, and, while the men smoked, the women spun, and the dogs slept, he entertained us with tales of heroes who knew the magic of the betel-nut, or with stories of spirits and their power over the lives of men.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The following are some of the tales heard first around the camp fire of the distant mountain village.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: One day Aponibolinayen and her sister-in-law went out to gather greens.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They walked to the woods to the place where the siksiklat grew, for the tender leaves of this vine are very good to eat.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Suddenly while searching about in the underbrush, Aponibolinayen cried out with joy, for she had found the vine, and she started to pick the leaves.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Pull as hard as she would, however, the leaves did not come loose, and all at once the vine wound itself around her body and began carrying her upward. [1]
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Far up through the air she went until she reached the sky, and there the vine set her down under a tree.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Aponibolinayen was so surprised to find herself in the sky that for some time she just sat and looked around, and then, hearing a rooster crow, she arose to see if she could find it.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Not far from where she had sat was a beautiful spring surrounded by tall betel-nut trees whose tops were pure gold.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Rare beads were the sands of the spring, and the place where the women set their jars when they came to dip water was a large golden plate.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As Aponibolinayen stood admiring the beauties of this spring, she beheld a small house nearby, and she was filled with fear lest the owner should find her there.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: She looked about for some means of escape and finally climbed to the top of a betel-nut tree and hid.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Now the owner of this house was Ini-init, [2] the Sun, but he was never at home in the daylight, for it was his duty to shine in the sky and give light to all the world.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: At the close of the day when the Big Star took his place in the sky to shine through the night, Ini-init returned to his house, but early the next morning he was always off again.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: From her place in the top of the betel-nut tree, Aponibolinayen saw the Sun when he came home at evening time, and again the next morning she saw him leave.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When she was sure that he was out of sight she climbed down and entered his dwelling, for she was very hungry.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: She cooked rice, and into a pot of boiling water she dropped a stick which immediately became fish, [3] so that she had all she wished to eat.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When she was no longer hungry, she lay down on the bed to sleep.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Now late in the afternoon Ini-init returned from his work and went to fish in the river near his house, and he caught a big fish.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: While he sat on the bank cleaning his catch, he happened to look up toward his house and was startled to see that it appeared to be on fire. [4] He hurried home, but when he reached the house he saw that it was not burning at all, and he entered.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: On his bed he beheld what looked like a flame of fire, but upon going closer he found that it was a beautiful woman fast asleep.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Ini-init stood for some time wondering what he should do, and then he decided to cook some food and invite this lovely creature to eat with him.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He put rice over the fire to boil and cut into pieces the fish he had caught.
rows.author: Compiled by Mabel Cook Cole from named Philippine traditions
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The noise of this awakened Aponibolinayen, and she slipped out of the house and back to the top of the betel-nut tree.

rows.text: After some time Aponibolinayen and the Sun were married, and every morning the Sun went to shine in the sky, and upon his return at night he found his supper ready for him.

rows.text: He began to be troubled, however, to know where the food came from, for though he brought home a fine fish every night, Aponibolinayen always refused to cook it.

rows.text: One night he watched her prepare their meal, and he saw that, instead of using the nice fish he had brought, she only dropped a stick into the pot of boiling water.

rows.text: "Why do you try to cook a stick?" asked Ini-init in surprise.

rows.text: "If you cook that stick for a month, it will not be soft," said Ini-init. "Take this fish that I caught in the net, for it will be good."

rows.text: But Aponibolinayen only laughed at him, and when they were ready to eat she took the cover off the pot and there was plenty of nice soft fish.

rows.text: The next night and the next, Aponibolinayen cooked the stick, and Ini-init became greatly troubled for he saw that though the stick always supplied them with fish, it never grew smaller.

rows.text: Finally he asked Aponibolinayen again why it was that she cooked the stick instead of the fish he brought, and she said:

rows.text: "Do you not know of the woman on earth who has magical power and can change things?"

rows.text: "Yes," answered the Sun, "and now I know that you have great power."

rows.text: This volume is reverently dedicated to all seekers of truth and lovers of wisdom
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda

rows.text: The translator's idea of rendering the Upanishads into clear simple English, accessible to Occidental readers, had its origin in a visit paid to a Boston friend in 1909.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The gentleman, then battling with a fatal malady, took from his library shelf a translation of the Upanishads and, opening it, expressed deep regret that the obscure and unfamiliar form shut from him what he felt to be profound and vital teaching.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda

rows.text: The desire to unlock the closed doors of this ancient treasure house, awakened at that time, led to a series of classes on the Upanishads at The Vedanta Centre of Boston during its early days in St.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The translation and commentary then given were transcribed and, after studious revision, were published in the Centre's monthly magazine, "The Message of the East," in 1913 and 1914..
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: So far as was consistent with a faithful rendering of the Sanskrit text, the Swami throughout his translation has sought to eliminate all that might seem obscure and confusing to the modern mind.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: While retaining in remarkable measure the rhythm and archaic force of the lines, he has tried not to sacrifice directness and simplicity of style.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Where he has been obliged to use the Sanskrit term for lack of an exact English equivalent, he has invariably interpreted it by a familiar English word in brackets; and everything has been done to remove the sense of strangeness in order that the Occidental reader may not feel himself an alien in the new regions of thought opened to him.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Even more has the Swami striven to keep the letter subordinate to the spirit.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To treat it as an object of mere intellectual curiosity is to cheat the world of its deeper message.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If mankind is to derive the highest benefit from a study of it, its appeal must be primarily to the spiritual consciousness; and one of the salient merits of the present translation lies in this, that the translator approaches his task not only with the grave concern of the careful scholar, but also with the profound reverence and fervor of the true devotee.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Upanishads represent the loftiest heights of ancient Indo-Aryan thought and culture.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They form the wisdom portion or Gnana-Kanda of the Vedas, as contrasted with the Karma-Kanda or sacrificial portion.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In each of the four great Vedas--known as Rik, Yajur, Sama and Atharva--there is a large portion which deals predominantly with rituals and ceremonials, and which has for its aim to show man how by the path of right action he may prepare himself for higher attainment.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Following this in each Veda is another portion called the Upanishad, which deals wholly with the essentials of philosophic discrimination and ultimate spiritual vision.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: For this reason the Upanishads are known as the Vedanta, that is, the end or final goal of wisdom (Veda, wisdom; anta, end).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Many claim that it is a compound Sanskrit word Upa-ni-shad, signifying "sitting at the feet or in the presence of a teacher"; while according to other authorities it means "to shatter" or "to destroy" the fetters of ignorance.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Whatever may have been the technical reason for selecting this name, it was chosen undoubtedly to give a picture of aspiring seekers "approaching" some wise Seer in the seclusion of an Himalayan forest, in order to learn of him the profoundest truths regarding the cosmic universe and God.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Because these teachings were usually given in the stillness of some distant retreat, where the noises of the world could not disturb the tranquillity of the contemplative life, they are known also as Aranyakas, Forest Books.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Another reason for this name may be found in the fact that they were intended especially for the Vanaprasthas (those who, having fulfilled all their duties in the world, had retired to the forest to devote themselves to spiritual study).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The form which the teaching naturally assumed was that of dialogue, a form later adopted by Plato and other Greek philosophers.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As nothing was written and all instruction was transmitted orally, the Upanishads are called Srutis, "what is heard." The term was also used in the sense of revealed, the Upanishads being regarded as direct revelations of God; while the Smritis, minor Scriptures "recorded through memory," were traditional works of purely human origin.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is a significant fact that nowhere in the Upanishads is mention made of any author or recorder.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: No date for the origin of the Upanishads can be fixed, because the written text does not limit their antiquity.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The teaching probably existed ages before it was set down in any written form.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The text itself bears evidence of this, because not infrequently in a dialogue between teacher and disciple the teacher quotes from earlier Scriptures now unknown to us.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As Professor Max Müller states in his lectures on the Vedanta Philosophy: "One feels certain that behind all these lightning-flashes of religious and philosophic thought there is a distant past, a dark background of which we shall never know the beginning." Some scholars place the Vedic period as far back as 4000 or 5000 B.C.; others from 2000 to 1400 B.C.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But even the most conservative admit that it antedates, by several centuries at least, the Buddhistic period which begins in the sixth century B.C.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The value of the Upanishads, however, does not rest upon their antiquity, but upon the vital message they contain for all times and all peoples.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The ennobling lessons of these Scriptures are as practical for the modern world as they were for the Indo-Aryans of the earliest Vedic age.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Their teachings are summed up in two Maha-Vakyam or "great sayings":--Tat twam asi (That thou art) and Aham Brahmasmi (I am Brahman).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This oneness of Soul and God lies at the very root of all Vedic thought, and it is this dominant ideal of the unity of all life and the oneness of Truth which makes the study of the Upanishads especially beneficial at the present moment.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: One of the most eminent of European Orientalists writes: "If we fix our attention upon it (this fundamental dogma of the Vedanta system) in its philosophical simplicity as the identity of God and the Soul, the Brahman and the Atman, it will be found to possess a significance reaching far beyond the Upanishads, their time and country; nay, we claim for it an inestimable value for the whole race of mankind.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Whatever new and unwonted paths the philosophy of the future may strike out, this principle will remain permanently unshaken and from it no deviation can possibly take place.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If ever a general solution is reached of the great riddle . . . the key can only be found where alone the secret of nature lies open to us from within, that is to say, in our innermost self.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It was here that for the first time the original thinkers of the Upanishads, to their immortal honor, found it...."
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The first introduction of the Upanishads to the Western world was through a translation into Persian made in the seventeenth century.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: More than a century later the distinguished French scholar, Anquetil Duperron, brought a copy of the manuscript from Persia to France and translated it into French and Latin.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Despite the distortions which must have resulted from transmission through two alien languages, the light of the thought still shone with such brightness that it drew from Schopenhauer the fervent words: "How entirely does the Oupnekhat (Upanishad) breathe throughout the holy spirit of the Vedas!
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: How is every one, who by a diligent study of its Persian Latin has become familiar with that incomparable book, stirred by that spirit to the very depth of his Soul!
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: From every sentence deep, original and sublime thoughts arise, and the whole is pervaded by a high and holy and earnest spirit." Again he says: "The access to (the Vedas) by means of the Upanishads is in my eyes the greatest privilege which this still young century (1818) may claim before all previous centuries." This testimony is borne out by the thoughtful American scholar, Thoreau, who writes: "What extracts from the Vedas I have read fall on me like the light of a higher and purer luminary which describes a loftier course through a purer stratum free from particulars, simple, universal."
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The first English translation was made by a learned Hindu, Raja Ram Mohun Roy (1775-1833).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Since that time there have been various European translations--French, German, Italian and English.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But a mere translation, however accurate and sympathetic, is not sufficient to make the Upanishads accessible to the Occidental mind.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Professor Max Müller after a lifetime of arduous labor in this field frankly confesses: "Modern words are round, ancient words are square, and we may as well hope to solve the quadrature of the circle, as to express adequately the ancient thought of the Vedas in modern English."
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Without a commentary it is practically impossible to understand either the spirit or the meaning of the Upanishads.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: They grew up essentially as text books of God-knowledge and Self-knowledge, and like all text books they need interpretation.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Being transmitted orally from teacher to disciple, the style was necessarily extremely condensed and in the form of aphorisms.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Yet if one has the perseverance to penetrate beneath these mere surface difficulties, one is repaid a hundredfold; for these ancient Sacred Books contain the most precious gems of spiritual thought.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
theme_evidence: Lời dẫn, đề tặng, tự thuật hoặc lịch sử xuất bản; giữ ngữ cảnh, không coi là danh ngôn của tác phẩm.
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Every Upanishad begins with a Peace Chant (Shanti-patha) to create the proper atmosphere of purity and serenity.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To study about God the whole nature must be prepared, so unitedly and with loving hearts teacher and disciples prayed to the Supreme Being for His grace and protection.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is not possible to comprehend the subtle problems of life unless the thought is tranquil and the energy concentrated.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
theme_evidence: Văn bản tôn giáo/đạo đức cần giữ ngữ cảnh; không tự biến thành quy luật tâm lý hoặc cam kết kết quả.
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Until our mind is withdrawn from the varied distractions and agitations of worldly affairs, we cannot enter into the spirit of higher religious study.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: No study is of avail so long as our inner being is not attuned.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We must hold a peaceful attitude towards all living things; and if it is lacking, we must strive fervently to cultivate it through suggestion by chanting or repeating some holy text.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The same lesson is taught by Jesus the Christ when He says: "If thou bring thy gift to the altar and there rememberest that thy brother hath aught against thee; leave there thy gift before the altar and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Bearing this lofty ideal of peace in our minds, let us try to make our hearts free from prejudice, doubt and intolerance, so that from these sacred writings we may draw in abundance inspiration, love and wisdom.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: This Upanishad desires its title from the opening words Isa-vasya, "God-covered." The use of Isa (Lord)--a more personal name of the Supreme Being than Brahman, Atman or Self, the names usually found in the Upanishads--constitutes one of its peculiarities.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It forms the closing chapter of the Yajur-Veda, known as Shukla (White).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Oneness of the Soul and God, and the value of both faith and works as means of ultimate attainment are the leading themes of this Upanishad.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The general teaching of the Upanishads is that works alone, even the highest, can bring only temporary happiness and must inevitably bind a man unless through them he gains knowledge of his real Self.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: To help him acquire this knowledge is the aim of this and all Upanishads.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: That (the Invisible-Absolute) is whole; whole is this (the visible phenomenal); from the Invisible Whole comes forth the visible whole.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Though the visible whole has come out from that Invisible Whole, yet the Whole remains unaltered.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The indefinite term "That" is used in the Upanishads to designate the Invisible-Absolute, because no word or name can fully define It.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: A finite object, like a table or a tree, can be defined; but God, who is infinite and unbounded, cannot be expressed by finite language.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Therefore the Rishis or Divine Seers, desirous not to limit the Unlimited, chose the indefinite term "That" to designate the Absolute.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: In the light of true wisdom the phenomenal and the Absolute are inseparable.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All existence is in the Absolute; and whatever exists, must exist in It; hence all manifestation is merely a modification of the One Supreme Whole, and neither increases nor diminishes It.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: All this, whatsoever exists in the universe, should be covered by the Lord.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: We cover all things with the Lord by perceiving the Divine Presence everywhere.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When the consciousness is firmly fixed in God, the conception of diversity naturally drops away; because the One Cosmic Existence shines through all things.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As we gain the light of wisdom, we cease to cling to the unrealities of this world and we find all our joy in the realm of Reality.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The word "enjoy" is also interpreted by the great commentator Sankaracharya as "protect," because knowledge of our true Self is the greatest protector and sustainer.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If we do not have this knowledge, we cannot be happy; because nothing on this external plane of phenomena is permanent or dependable.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He who is rich in the knowledge of the Self does not covet external power or possession.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If one should desire to live in this world a hundred years, one should live performing Karma (righteous deeds).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: By doing this, Karma (the fruits of thy actions) will not defile thee.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: If a man still clings to long life and earthly possessions, and is therefore unable to follow the path of Self-knowledge (Gnana-Nishta) as prescribed in the first Mantram (text), then he may follow the path of right action (Karma-Nishta).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Karma here means actions performed without selfish motive, for the sake of the Lord alone.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When a man performs actions clinging blindly to his lower desires, then his actions bind him to the plane of ignorance or the plane of birth and death; but when the same actions are performed with surrender to God, they purify and liberate him.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: After leaving their bodies, they who have killed the Self go to the worlds of the Asuras, covered with blinding ignorance.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The idea of rising to bright regions as a reward for well-doers, and of falling into realms of darkness as a punishment for evil-doers is common to all great religions.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: But Vedanta claims that this condition of heaven and hell is only temporary; because our actions, being finite, can produce only a finite result.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: What does it mean "to kill the Self?" How can the immortal Soul ever be destroyed?
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Those who hold themselves under the sway of ignorance, who serve the flesh and neglect the Atman or the real Self, are not able to perceive the effulgent and indestructible nature of their Soul; hence they fall into the realm where the Soul light does not shine.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Here the Upanishad shows that the only hell is absence of knowledge.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: As long as man is overpowered by the darkness of ignorance, he is the slave of Nature and must accept whatever comes as the fruit of his thoughts and deeds.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When he strays into the path of unreality, the Sages declare that he destroys himself; because he who clings to the perishable body and regards it as his true Self must experience death many times.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: A finite object can be taken from one place and put in another, but it can only occupy one space at a time.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: The Atman, however, is present everywhere; hence, though one may run with the greatest swiftness to overtake It, already It is there before him.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Even the all-pervading air must be supported by this Self, since It is infinite; and as nothing can live without breathing air, all living things must draw their life from the Cosmic Self.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is near to those who have the power to understand It, for It dwells in the heart of every one; but It seems far to those whose mind is covered by the clouds of sensuality and self-delusion.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: It is within, because It is the innermost Soul of all creatures; and It is without as the essence of the whole external universe, infilling it like the all-pervading ether.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from It (the Self).
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He who perceives all beings as the Self for him how can there be delusion or grief, when he sees this oneness (everywhere)?
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: He who perceives the Self everywhere never shrinks from anything, because through his higher consciousness he feels united with all life.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: When a man sees God in all beings and all beings in God, and also God dwelling in his own Soul, how can he hate any living thing?
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Grief and delusion rest upon a belief in diversity, which leads to competition and all forms of selfishness.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: With the realization of oneness, the sense of diversity vanishes and the cause of misery is removed.
rows.author: Translated from Sanskrit by Swami Paramananda
rows.rights_status_observed: Public domain in the USA per Project Gutenberg record; jurisdiction review required for redistribution.

rows.text: Dhritirashtra: Ranged thus for battle on the sacred plain-- On Kurukshetra--say, Sanjaya! say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?
